site.title: Mehetabel Gyebi Aquinas, chef
site.description: Mehetabel Gyebi Aquinas is a chef in Accra who cooks West African food with a modern hand, runs the kitchen, and then tells the world about what came out of it.

oneGrain.label: One grain
oneGrain.headline: It starts with **one grain**.
oneGrain.body: My grandmother's kitchen in Koforidua, age nine. One blackened pot, one wooden spoon worn flat on one side, and a rule: you do not lift the lid until she says so.

manyGrains.label: Many grains
manyGrains.headline: One grain is nothing. **A thousand is a meal.**
manyGrains.body: A Wednesday special is sixty boxes of jollof, each one leaving the counter the way the first one did. Scale is not louder cooking. It is the same care, repeated until nobody can tell which box was number one.
manyGrains.interactionHint: The grains settle into the number

ingredients.label: The ingredients
ingredients.headline: Rice is **only the beginning**.
ingredients.body: Everything else in the pot is a decision. The tomato is where I shop, the onion is how long I am willing to wait, the pepper is who I am cooking for. Read them and you have read how I work.
ingredients.interactionHint: Tap an ingredient to read what it stands for

fire.label: The fire
fire.headline: Technique is what **the fire reveals**.
fire.body: Nine years at the stove, from scrubbing cassava in a chop bar to running my own kitchen in Kumasi. Fire does not care about your plans. It taught me to cut faster, taste sooner, and say sorry to a pot only once.

photo.alt: Mehetabel in her apron, laughing, caught mid-service

fire.interactionHint: Hover or touch to raise the heat

secret.label: The secret ingredient
secret.headline: Everyone asks. **It's love.**
secret.handwritingAlt: The word love, in Mehetabel's handwriting
secret.paragraph: I cook because the kitchen is the one place where I know exactly what to do with my hands. I cook for the person who had a long day and did not expect to be looked after. I cook for my grandmother, who is not here to taste it, and for the table of strangers who will become friends by the second course. When the plate lands I want you to go quiet for a moment, the way people do when something is true. Then I want you to look up, find whoever you came with, and push the plate toward them so they can try it too. That is the whole job.

pot.label: The pot
pot.headline: Then **you wait**.
pot.body: The smoky layer at the bottom of the pot cannot be rushed and cannot be faked. Neither can a kitchen. The largest brigade I have led was fourteen cooks, and I ask three things of every one of them: taste everything, call it when you are behind, and leave the station cleaner than the person before you.

photo.alt: Mehetabel in her apron, smiling, one hand on her hip

pot.interactionHint: Scrub the timeline to watch the colour spread

plate.label: The plate
plate.headline: Eaten with **the eyes first**.
plate.body: A plate is read before it is tasted. Where the colour sits, how much white space is left, which way the chicken faces: all of it is a sentence, and I want mine to be short and clear.

table.label: The table
table.headline: Food is only finished **when it's shared**.
table.body: Twelve events this year, from a dinner for eight on a rooftop in Osu to a wedding where the table ran the full length of the garden. The food is the reason people sit down. The table is the reason they stay.

stat.caption: people fed at events this year

photo.alt: A long outdoor table set for 60 guests, seen from above, before anyone has sat down

story.label: The story
story.headline: A dish nobody hears about **is a secret**.
story.body: I studied public relations and marketing before I ever ran a kitchen, and the two have never been separate for me. Three menu launches, five campaigns, and a Wednesday special that people had heard about before they tasted it. The cooking earns the attention. The telling makes sure it arrives.

work.body: Menus I have written, tables I have served, launches I have run, and the campaigns that put them in front of people.

ingredients.name: Tomatoes
ingredients.note: Tuesday mornings at Agbogbloshie market, the same two women for six years. A pale tomato makes a pale pot, and no amount of heat will fix it. The dish is decided before the gas is on.

ingredients.name: Onions
ingredients.note: Onions are not done until they are done. The first time I rushed them for a table of forty I learned that sweetness takes exactly as long as it takes, and so does a cook who is still learning.

ingredients.name: Peppers
ingredients.note: Heat without hurt. I taste, adjust, taste again, and I am always seasoning for the quietest person at the table, not the loudest.

ingredients.name: Spices
ingredients.note: The blends I grew up with, the ones I found in other people's kitchens, and the discipline of keeping them from shouting over each other. A spice should be recognised, not announced.

ingredients.name: Stock
ingredients.note: What is in the pot changes with the month. I write menus backwards: first what is good in the market this week, then what to do with it.

projects.name: The Wednesday special
projects.what: A weekly special built around what Kumasi's markets are full of that week: smoked fish one Wednesday, the first good tomatoes the next. One pot of jollof, costed to the gram, cooked by me, boxed with chicken, and gone by the time it was cool enough to pack.
projects.outcome: One hundred and thirty boxes in the first month, a list of regulars who order by Tuesday night, and a food cost that came in two points under target.

images.alt: Service: a box of jollof and chicken filled from a tray of roasted chicken and sausages

projects.name: A garden wedding for 60
projects.scale: 60 guests, 4 courses, one tent, one generator
projects.what: Four courses for sixty people in a garden in East Legon, with a brigade of three and a kitchen built that morning under a tent. The generator failed between the second and third courses. We finished the jollof on charcoal, which is how it should have been cooked in the first place.
projects.outcome: All sixty served within eleven minutes of each course call. Three bookings from guests at the table before the cake was cut.

images.alt: The wedding table set under the trees, before guests arrived

projects.name: Launching the Wednesday special
projects.what: A dish is a secret until somebody tells it. I planned the content around one image a day from the kitchen, cooked and shot by me, wrote every caption, and sent the first Wednesday's boxes to twelve people who would talk about them.
projects.outcome: Reach in launch week went from fifty to three hundred and thirty. Twelve reposts and mentions. Boxes more than tripled in the month that followed.

images.alt: A hand with tongs serving jollof and a chicken leg into a takeaway box

projects.name: Six Sundays, a palm oil campaign
projects.role: Recipe developer and face of the campaign
projects.what: A Ghanaian palm oil brand wanted to reach younger home cooks who had stopped using it. I developed six Sunday recipes, one a week, that treated palm oil as an ingredient with a flavour rather than a fat you hide. I cooked, shot and fronted every one of them.
projects.outcome: Two hundred and forty thousand views across the run, a sell-out of the one-litre bottle in two Accra supermarkets, and a second campaign commissioned before the first had ended.

images.alt: A still from the campaign, red palm oil poured over a bowl of rice

game.title: The jollof timer
game.intro: Ninety seconds, one pot. Add each ingredient at the right moment, keep the heat in the band, and decide when to lift the lid.
rules: Add in order: oil, onions, pepper base, stock, rice, then cover.
Keep the heat in the band shown. Too hot for too long and it burns. Too timid and it stays pale.
After the lid goes on, a short spell of high heat gives you the smoky bottom. Push it too far and you lose everything.
Lift the lid when you think it is ready, or let the clock run out.

recipe.title: Mehetabel's jollof
recipe.intro: Six ingredients are hidden on this page: inside a grain, behind a photo, in the fire, in a skill, in a project and in the footer. Find all six and the recipe is yours to print.

ingredients.label: 500 g long-grain parboiled rice, washed until the water runs clear
6 ripe plum tomatoes, 2 tbsp tomato paste
2 red bell peppers, 1 scotch bonnet, seeds in if you are brave
ingredients.hint: Hold the heat high in the fire.

ingredients.label: 2 onions, one blended and one sliced thin
ingredients.hint: One skill on the pantry shelf has it.

ingredients.label: 600 ml chicken stock, 1 bay leaf, a few sprigs of thyme
100 ml vegetable oil, 1 tsp curry powder, a pinch of white pepper

method: Blend the tomatoes, peppers, scotch bonnet and one onion. Reduce the blend in a dry pan until it darkens and thickens. This is the step people skip, and it is the step that matters.
Heat the oil, soften the sliced onion, add the paste and fry until the oil turns red and separates.
Add the reduced blend, curry powder, thyme and bay. Cook until the raw tomato smell is gone and the sauce tastes like it has somewhere to be.
Add the stock and the washed rice. Season. Bring to a boil, then cover tightly with foil and a lid.
Lowest heat for 25 minutes. Do not open the lid. My grandmother is watching.
For the smoky bottom, raise the heat for the last three minutes. Rest ten minutes, then fluff from the edges in.
recipe.signoff: Cooked and written by Mehetabel Gyebi Aquinas
